concept.name: Battery
concept.wording: A battery: two long-range pieces on the same file, rank or diagonal, with nothing of their own between them. The front piece can capture and the rear one recaptures, so the pair attacks with more force than either alone.
cautions: Ordering matters: queen in front of rook is usually worse than rook in front of queen, because the more valuable piece meets the defenders first.
Two line pieces on one line are only a battery if the line ARRIVES somewhere. Stacked behind their own pawns they combine nothing, and the bare geometry fires on nearly half of all positions.

concepts.name: Doubled pawns
concepts.wording: Doubled pawns: two friendly pawns on one file. They cannot defend each other and the rear one is blocked, but the capture that created them usually bought something — a file, the bishop pair, or central control.
cautions: Doubled central pawns frequently increase control and are an asset.
The exchange that doubles them often yields the bishop pair or a usable file, which is the whole point.

concepts.name: Semi-open file
concepts.wording: A semi-open file: no pawn of your own, one of the opponent's. It is often more useful than a fully open file, because it is asymmetric - the enemy pawn is a target that cannot move sideways, and you can usually attack it more times than it can be defended.
cautions: A semi-open file with no entry square and a defensible pawn achieves nothing.
Where the enemy pawn can advance freely, the file is a route rather than a lever.

altConcept.name: Passed pawn

cautions: PROVEN EXCEPTION to Tarrasch's 'rook behind the passed pawn': in the Vancura configuration — a rook pawn on the sixth with the attacking rook in front of it — putting the rook behind the pawn LOSES. concepts.name: Battery
concepts.wording: A battery: two long-range pieces on the same file, rank or diagonal, with nothing of their own between them. The front piece can capture and the rear one recaptures, so the pair attacks with more force than either alone.
cautions: Ordering matters: queen in front of rook is usually worse than rook in front of queen, because the more valuable piece meets the defenders first.
Two line pieces on one line are only a battery if the line ARRIVES somewhere. Stacked behind their own pawns they combine nothing, and the bare geometry fires on nearly half of all positions.

concepts.wording: A discovered attack: two attacks for one move — whatever the moving piece does, and whatever the piece behind it now hits. The moving piece is comparatively free, because the opponent has to deal with the revealed threat.
cautions: A discovery is worthless if the unmasked line hits nothing of value.
In a discovered check the moving piece may stand en prise with impunity — normal safety reasoning does not apply to it.

concepts.name: Hanging piece
concepts.why: It leaves the queen on c6 hanging — it can simply be taken.
concepts.wording: A piece that is attacked and can be captured for free — undefended, or defended fewer times than it is attacked.
cautions: A hanging piece may be a sacrifice offered on purpose. SEE says the material is winnable; it does not say taking is right.
In a lost position, giving material to reach a fortress or a perpetual can be correct.

concepts.name: Outpost
concepts.wording: An advanced square, usually protected by a pawn, that no enemy pawn can attack — so a piece placed there cannot be driven away. Sources disagree on whether an open or half-open file behind it is part of the definition.
cautions: An outpost that can be neutralised by an equal exchange confers little. Check what can capture the occupant before naming it.
Occupying is not obligatory. The THREAT of occupying can bind the defender while the piece does something else.

concepts.name: Bad bishop
concepts.wording: A bad bishop — its own pawns sit on the squares it travels on, so its diagonals are blocked from the inside and the squares they leave uncovered are ones the bishop cannot use either. The cures are a pawn break, a trade, or getting the bishop outside the chain.
cautions: Suba's active bad bishop: outside the pawn chain, a structurally bad bishop is often equal or better than a knight.
A bad bishop defending a colour complex is doing essential work and should not be traded off casually.

concepts.name: King safety
concepts.wording: King safety: count the attackers that can reach the king's area against the defenders already there. One or two is normal; three against a damaged shield is when sacrifices start to work.
cautions: An exposed king is not a losing king. In a proven drawn ending both kings stand in the open with no pawn shelter, and centralising them is correct - see the recorded counterexample.
An exposed king with no attackers left is an ACTIVE king, and in the endgame that is what you want.

cautions: Active pieces do not guarantee compensation. The Halloween Gambit position in this base has genuinely active pieces and evaluates 1.75 worse.
Passive defence is sometimes objectively correct, particularly where a known drawing set-up requires it.

concepts.name: Pawn break
concepts.wording: A pawn break: an advance into contact with an enemy pawn, played to open a file or a diagonal for the pieces behind it, or to force the opponent's structure to commit. It is not played to win a pawn.
cautions: A break that opens lines for a better-developed opponent helps them.
Some positions are won by NOT breaking — keeping the tension is itself a plan, and the threat can be worth more than the move.

concepts.name: Blockade
concepts.wording: Blockade: park a piece directly in front of an enemy pawn so it cannot advance. A knight is the ideal blockader because it keeps all its power from the square; a queen is the worst, because any minor piece evicts her.
cautions: A blockade that ties down a piece needed elsewhere is a liability.
Blockading with a heavy piece is expensive and usually temporary.

concepts.name: Isolated queen's pawn

cautions: An isolated queen's pawn is not a weakness on sight. In the standard position measured here the side with the isolani is slightly better (+0.14).
The blanket rule 'trade pieces against an IQP' has an important qualification: trade MINOR pieces, but keep a queen and a rook, or there is nothing left to attack the pawn with.

concepts.name: Hanging pawns

cautions: Where the pair can advance profitably, they are a space-gaining asset rather than a weakness.
With enough piece activity the structure is fully sound; the 'weak by nature' framing is a starting assessment, not a verdict.

altConcept.name: Blockade
altConcept.wording: Blockade: park a piece directly in front of an enemy pawn so it cannot advance. A knight is the ideal blockader because it keeps all its power from the square; a queen is the worst, because any minor piece evicts her.
cautions: A blockade that ties down a piece needed elsewhere is a liability.
Blockading with a heavy piece is expensive and usually temporary.

concepts.name: Discovered attack

cautions: A discovery is worthless if the unmasked line hits nothing of value.
In a discovered check the moving piece may stand en prise with impunity — normal safety reasoning does not apply to it.

concepts.name: Pawn break
concepts.wording: A pawn break: an advance into contact with an enemy pawn, played to open a file or a diagonal for the pieces behind it, or to force the opponent's structure to commit. It is not played to win a pawn.
cautions: A break that opens lines for a better-developed opponent helps them.
Some positions are won by NOT breaking — keeping the tension is itself a plan, and the threat can be worth more than the move.

concepts.name: Control of the centre

Ceding the centre is not always right either — against proper support it just loses space.

concepts.name: Material imbalance
concepts.wording: A material imbalance: the sides hold different kinds of material rather than different amounts. The 1/3/3/5/9 scale stops applying, and the question becomes which pieces the position suits.
cautions: MEASURED 2026-09-02: a knight against a bishop is not an imbalance by this record's own preferred numbers - Kaufman puts a knight and an UNPAIRED bishop at the same 3.5 - and the matcher fired on every such swap, 42.1% of the 788 shipped positions. It is a third name for a fact `bishop-pair` and `bad-bishop` already report. The exception is the pair itself, which Kaufman does separate (7.5 against 7.0), so two bishops against two knights is still reported. 42.1% -> 35.5%.
Values shift with the amount of material: minor pieces are worth more pawns with a full board, rooks more with an empty one.

concept.wording: Promotion: a pawn arriving on the eighth rank is replaced immediately, as part of the same move, by a piece of its own colour. The choice is free and unlimited — a side may have several queens — and it is not confined to pieces already captured.
cautions: Promotion is compulsory: a pawn may not remain a pawn.
Underpromotion to a rook avoids stalemate where a queen would cause it; underpromotion to a knight gains a check or fork unavailable to a queen.

concepts.wording: One piece attacks two or more enemy units at once, so only one can be saved.

concepts.name: Hanging piece

concepts.name: Rook on the seventh rank

concepts.name: Pawn break
concepts.wording: A pawn break: an advance into contact with an enemy pawn, played to open a file or a diagonal for the pieces behind it, or to force the opponent's structure to commit. It is not played to win a pawn.

Some positions are won by NOT breaking — keeping the tension is itself a plan, and the threat can be worth more than the move.

cautions: Suba's active bad bishop: outside the pawn chain, a structurally bad bishop is often equal or better than a knight.
A bad bishop defending a colour complex is doing essential work and should not be traded off casually.

cautions: PROVEN EXCEPTION to Tarrasch's 'rook behind the passed pawn': in the Vancura configuration — a rook pawn on the sixth with the attacking rook in front of it — putting the rook behind the pawn LOSES. Tablebase-verified on a pair differing only in the defending rook's square: beside the pawn is a draw, behind it is a loss in 63. See `vancura-position`.
A blockaded passer that ties down its owner's pieces is a liability, not an asset. Nimzowitsch's blockade rule is right about half the time, which is the honest figure.

concepts.name: The bishop pair
concepts.wording: The bishop pair: a single bishop is blind to half the board, and two together cover everything. Statistically worth about half a pawn beyond the two bishops separately, and strongest in open positions.
cautions: In a locked position the pair may be worth nothing and a knight may be better.
A bishop shut in by its own pawns does not contribute to the pair.

concepts.name: King safety
concepts.wording: King safety: count the attackers that can reach the king's area against the defenders already there. One or two is normal; three against a damaged shield is when sacrifices start to work.
cautions: An exposed king is not a losing king. In a proven drawn ending both kings stand in the open with no pawn shelter, and centralising them is correct - see the recorded counterexample.
An exposed king with no attackers left is an ACTIVE king, and in the endgame that is what you want.

concepts.name: Pawn break
concepts.wording: A pawn break: an advance into contact with an enemy pawn, played to open a file or a diagonal for the pieces behind it, or to force the opponent's structure to commit. It is not played to win a pawn.
cautions: A break that opens lines for a better-developed opponent helps them.

cautions: Suba's active bad bishop: outside the pawn chain, a structurally bad bishop is often equal or better than a knight.
A bad bishop defending a colour complex is doing essential work and should not be traded off casually.

cautions: A trapped piece may escape by a desperado capture, or by a counter-threat that gains the tempo it needs.

moves.text: Forced — it is the only legal move.

The bishop pair: a single bishop is blind to half the board, and two together cover everything. Statistically worth about half a pawn beyond the two bishops separately, and strongest in open positions.

concept.name: The bishop pair
concept.wording: The bishop pair: a single bishop is blind to half the board, and two together cover everything. Statistically worth about half a pawn beyond the two bishops separately, and strongest in open positions.
cautions: In a locked position the pair may be worth nothing and a knight may be better.
A bishop shut in by its own pawns does not contribute to the pair.

why.mistake: Black played h6. The position was clearly worse for White before it and is clearly better after it, with best play.
why.point: The engine calls the position clearly better for White.

altConcept.name: Skewer
altConcept.why: The queen on b4 has to move, and the pawn on b7 behind it falls.
altConcept.wording: A skewer: a line attack with the MORE valuable unit in front. It moves, and what stands behind it is taken. The inverse of a pin, and it wins material immediately rather than paralysing.
cautions: If the front piece moves along the same line it may keep defending the piece behind.

concepts.name: Passed pawn
concepts.wording: A passed pawn: no enemy pawn ahead of it on its file or either neighbour, so only pieces can stop it. Its worth depends almost entirely on whether it can advance — a permanently blockaded passer is a liability rather than an asset.
cautions: PROVEN EXCEPTION to Tarrasch's 'rook behind the passed pawn': in the Vancura configuration — a rook pawn on the sixth with the attacking rook in front of it — putting the rook behind the pawn LOSES. Tablebase-verified on a pair differing only in the defending rook's square: beside the pawn is a draw, behind it is a loss in 63. See `vancura-position`.
A blockaded passer that ties down its owner's pieces is a liability, not an asset. Nimzowitsch's blockade rule is right about half the time, which is the honest figure.

concepts.name: Sacrifice
concepts.wording: A sacrifice. First ask whether the material comes back by force: if it does, calculate it and stop worrying. If it does not, you are judging the compensation instead.
cautions: A capture the engine happens to like is not a sacrifice. The repo's own definition is the right one: material that CAN be taken and is offered anyway, measured by SEE.
A sham sacrifice is not really a sacrifice at all; treating it as one invites judgement where calculation was required.

It comes with check, so the reply is not a free move. An isolated queen's pawn. It cannot be defended by a pawn and the square in front is a permanent hole — but it gives central space, half-open c- and e-files, and outposts beside it. It is an asset while pieces are on and a liability once they come off.

concept.name: Isolated queen's pawn
concept.wording: An isolated queen's pawn. It cannot be defended by a pawn and the square in front is a permanent hole — but it gives central space, half-open c- and e-files, and outposts beside it. It is an asset while pieces are on and a liability once they come off.
cautions: An isolated queen's pawn is not a weakness on sight. In the standard position measured here the side with the isolani is slightly better (+0.14).
The blanket rule 'trade pieces against an IQP' has an important qualification: trade MINOR pieces, but keep a queen and a rook, or there is nothing left to attack the pawn with.

It leaves the pawn on a7 hanging — it can simply be taken. It comes with check, so the reply is not a free move. One piece attacks two or more enemy units at once, so only one can be saved.

concept.name: Fork
concept.why: The queen on a6 forks the king on c8 and the pawn on a7.
concept.wording: One piece attacks two or more enemy units at once, so only one can be saved.
cautions: A fork wins nothing if the forking piece can be taken, or if every target is adequately defended and cheaper than the forker.
A relative fork can be met by a zwischenzug; an absolute fork cannot.

It comes with check, so the reply is not a free move. Opposite-coloured bishops: the bishops can never contest the same squares, so the defender can blockade on their own colour and the attacker's bishop can never challenge it. One extra pawn usually draws and two often do — on one wing. Passed pawns far enough apart beat a lone bishop, because it has to choose.

concept.name: Opposite-coloured bishops
concept.wording: Opposite-coloured bishops: the bishops can never contest the same squares, so the defender can blockade on their own colour and the attacker's bishop can never challenge it. One extra pawn usually draws and two often do — on one wing. Passed pawns far enough apart beat a lone bishop, because it has to choose.
cautions: The drawish rule is an endgame rule. With queens and rooks on, opposite bishops favour the attacker.
Three files of separation between passed pawns usually wins despite the bishops.

It leaves the pawn on a7 hanging — it can simply be taken. It comes with check, so the reply is not a free move. A piece that is attacked and can be captured for free — undefended, or defended fewer times than it is attacked.

concept.name: Hanging piece
concept.why: It leaves the pawn on a7 hanging — it can simply be taken.
concept.wording: A piece that is attacked and can be captured for free — undefended, or defended fewer times than it is attacked.
cautions: A hanging piece may be a sacrifice offered on purpose. SEE says the material is winnable; it does not say taking is right.
In a lost position, giving material to reach a fortress or a perpetual can be correct.

moves.text: The king is in check and has to answer it. It is the toughest try — nothing else does better.

It comes with check, so the reply is not a free move. King safety: count the attackers that can reach the king's area against the defenders already there. One or two is normal; three against a damaged shield is when sacrifices start to work.

concept.name: King safety
concept.wording: King safety: count the attackers that can reach the king's area against the defenders already there. One or two is normal; three against a damaged shield is when sacrifices start to work.
cautions: An exposed king is not a losing king. In a proven drawn ending both kings stand in the open with no pawn shelter, and centralising them is correct - see the recorded counterexample.
An exposed king with no attackers left is an ACTIVE king, and in the endgame that is what you want.

why.point: White is a piece down on material, though the engine calls the position only level.
